news.articleText: Release Number 9321-26 CFTC and USDA Sign MOU to Protect Integrity of American Agricultural Markets November 04, 2026 WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the U.S. Department of Agriculture today announced their signing of a Memorandum of Understanding intended to safeguard the integrity of U.S. agricultural markets. The MOU will allow the CFTC and USDA to harmonize policies and practices to better share information and increase access to risk management tools. The agreement will also assist both agencies with monitoring and identifying structural or potential systematic risks, among other things. “For decades, America’s agricultural community has relied on our markets to hedge risk, manage uncertainty, and plan for the future,” said CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig. “I’m proud that the CFTC and USDA have formalized this partnership through an MOU that will strengthen protections for America’s farmers, ranchers, and producers while expanding opportunities to manage risk through more efficient data sharing. I commend Secretary Rollins for her partnership and commitment to a more coordinated regulatory approach that safeguards the integrity of our markets and ensures they continue serving the agricultural community that feeds and clothes our nation.” “Faster and more transparent data sharing between USDA and CFTC is critical to helping our farmers and ranchers navigate an ever-changing market,” said USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins. “This MOU builds upon USDA’s ongoing data modernization efforts and allows our agencies to collaboratively identify risks and improve responses to market events. Breaking down barriers between government agencies to deliver for our customers is a hallmark of this administration and I am looking forward to the successes this MOU will bring.” -CFTC-

news.title: CFTC Secures Court Order Directing Texas Man and His Company to Pay Over $13 Million in Commodities Fraud
news.verification: Birincil kaynak
news.titleTr: CFTC Secures Court Order Directing Texas Man and His Company to Pay Over $13 Million in Commodities Fraud
news.articleText: Release Number 9320-26 CFTC Secures Court Order Directing Texas Man and His Company to Pay Over $13 Million in Commodities Fraud November 03, 2026 WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today announced the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas entered a default judgment against defendants Walter Dunning Larrick III and Cambridge Financial Advisors LLC for their participation in a commodities fraud scheme. In entering the default judgment, the court found the defendants fraudulently solicited and misappropriated more than $3 million from participants. The court found the defendants falsely represented they would use participant funds to trade futures and options, including those involving natural gas, oil, and gold; made material misrepresentations and omissions about the profitability of commodity trading with them; and issued false account statements to conceal their misconduct. The court further found the defendants misappropriated participant funds by making payments to existing participants in a manner akin to a Ponzi scheme, paying Larrick’s personal expenses, and sending funds to offshore accounts in Costa Rica. The court ordered the defendants to pay a $9,767,625 civil monetary penalty and $3,255,875 in restitution. It also permanently enjoined them from further violations of the Commodity Exchange Act and Commission regulations, as charged, and imposed permanent trading and registration bans. The default judgment resolves all claims in the CFTC’s 2023 complaint. [See CFTC Press Release No. 8768-23.] -CFTC-

news.title: CFTC Chairman Selig Releases Statement on Equity Perpetual Futures
news.verification: Birincil kaynak
news.titleTr: CFTC Chairman Selig Releases Statement on Equity Perpetual Futures
news.articleText: Release Number 9319-26 CFTC Chairman Selig Releases Statement on Equity Perpetual Futures November 03, 2026 WASHINGTON — CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig today released a statement announcing that perpetual futures contracts on individual equity securities can begin trading for the first time on designated contract markets that are dually registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as notice-registered national securities exchanges to trade security futures products. Key excerpts from Chairman Selig’s statement: “Today, perpetual futures contracts on individual equity securities (the ‘Equity Perps’) can begin trading for the first time on CFTC-registered exchanges. … “This expansion marks a significant step towards allowing U.S. market participants, consistent with applicable law, to avail themselves of the advantages of perpetual futures that have led to their emergence as widely sought tools for risk-management and price-discovery. I believe that bringing these types of innovative products into our regulated markets ensures that American investors and traders can access these products within the protections of the CFTC’s proven regulatory framework, rather than being forced to turn to offshore, and often unregulated, venues. … “The Equity Perps build on the foundation of the [Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000] and the [CFTC-SEC Memorandum of Understanding]. For too long, regulatory uncertainty left innovative products, such as security futures and equity perpetual futures, stranded in what SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins has aptly described as a regulatory ‘no man’s land’ due to a lack of harmonization between the agencies. The CFTC and SEC have turned the page on that era, and are committed to delivering regulatory clarity for innovative products and a clear path to market, rather than more casualties of jurisdictional disputes.” Read Chairman Selig’s full statement here. -CFTC-

news.title: CFTC to Host Roundtable on 24/7 Trading
news.verification: Birincil kaynak
news.titleTr: CFTC to Host Roundtable on 24/7 Trading
news.articleText: Release Number 9318-26 CFTC to Host Roundtable on 24/7 Trading October 28, 2026 WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today announced it will host an industry roundtable Dec. 15 to discuss issues related to the viability of derivatives markets moving to 24/7 trading. The dialogue will build upon the CFTC’s Request for Comment earlier this summer on 24/7 trading. The CFTC’s roundtable will provide a public venue for dialogue on the evolving market structures shaping derivatives markets, including overnight trading, tokenization, infrastructure and staffing needs, and operational readiness. Participants will convene from across the industry to discuss how the Commission can promote responsible innovation while protecting market participants and preserving the integrity and resilience of U.S. derivatives markets. “I have been consistently clear: under my leadership, the CFTC will not take a one‑size‑fits‑all approach to 24/7 trading. Market structure evolves best through thoughtful and responsible progress, and that’s exactly why we’re hosting a roundtable to hear directly from industry on their views for 24/7 trading across different asset classes,” Chairman Selig said. The roundtable will take place at CFTC’s headquarters in Washington. Information regarding the agenda, speakers, and registration will be posted at a later date. This event will be open to the public and livestreamed on CFTC.gov. Please note the number of in-person participants may be limited, and visitors will be subject to security checks. Members of the public are welcome to submit speaker nominations to [email protected]. -CFTC-

news.title: ICYMI: Agricultural Leaders and Market Participants Join CFTC Chairman Selig in Overland Park, Kansas for AgCon 2026
news.verification: Birincil kaynak
news.titleTr: ICYMI: Agricultural Leaders and Market Participants Join CFTC Chairman Selig in Overland Park, Kansas for AgCon 2026
news.articleText: Release Number 9317-26 ICYMI: Agricultural Leaders and Market Participants Join CFTC Chairman Selig in Overland Park, Kansas for AgCon 2026 October 27, 2026 WASHINGTON — Last week, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Risk Management Center at Kansas State University co-hosted the 2026 Agricultural Commodity Futures Conference (AgCon) in Overland Park, Kansas. The two-day conference brought together industry leaders, policymakers, and market participants to examine critical issues facing the agricultural economy, developments in derivatives markets, and the risk management tools American farmers, ranchers, and agribusinesses depend on. Conference Highlights CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig joined K-State President Richard Linton to welcome participants on opening day. CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig addressed conference attendees, “I have spent a lot of time this year traveling around the country and talking to farmers and ranchers working hard each day to provide the food, feed, and fiber we depend on throughout our country and the world. I’ve met with farmers, ranchers, agribusinesses, and energy producers in Iowa, Texas, Nebraska, South Carolina, and Florida, and now, I’m with all of you here in Kansas.” [Watch Chairman Selig’s full remarks here.] Following Chairman Selig’s remarks, panelists examined the relationship between cash and derivatives markets, evolving commodity contracts, and the importance of effective hedging tools for agricultural producers. There were also panels where industry representatives addressed access to agricultural credit and the financial challenges facing producers and merchants. Additional afternoon discussions focused on rising production costs, fluctuating commodity prices, supply chain disruptions, and broader pressures on the farm economy. In addition, conference participants engaged in discussions about emerging market developments, including perpetual futures, 24/7 trading, and tokenized collateral, and their implications for agricultural risk management. CFTC Chief Advisor Alex Titus and White House Council of Economic Advisers Member Aaron Hedlund also examined the U.S. economic outlook, agricultural trade, and policies shaping American agriculture. The first day concluded with a keynote address from U.S. Department of Agriculture Deputy Secretary Stephen Vaden. U.S. Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas opened the second day with a morning keynote address on agricultural policy and legislative priorities facing American producers. The morning continued with discussions on agricultural prediction markets, the use of data in modern commodity markets, and developments in event contracts. In addition, panelists examined superintelligence, information advantages, and market integrity, including the implications of emerging technologies for market participants and regulators. Chairman Selig joined Futures Industry Association President and CEO Walt Lukken for a fireside chat examining the Commission’s priorities, the evolving regulatory landscape, and developments shaping derivatives markets. The conference concluded with discussions on enhancing public understanding of markets through data and customer education, followed by a panel examining clearing, market access, and the role of intermediaries in derivatives markets. Chairman Selig delivered closing remarks, concluding AgCon2026. -CFTC-

items.summary: The 82-year-old was placed under house detention in Florida last week after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.

items.titleTr: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor
items.summaryTr: The 82-year-old was placed under house detention in Florida last week after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.
items.articleText: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor - Published Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents. Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning. US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show. Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device. The BBC has contacted his representatives. Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court". He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician". "Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday. "We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added. Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said. Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material. Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material. In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old. Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention. He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ. FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions". Markle has called the allegations "sick lies". He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated. The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls. In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed." She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children". items.summary: The project warned that installations running older versions were vulnerable and urged operators to replace potentially exposed credentials even after upgrading.

items.titleTr: LNbits rushes emergency patch after reported Bitcoin wallet thefts
items.summaryTr: The project warned that installations running older versions were vulnerable and urged operators to replace potentially exposed credentials even after upgrading.
items.articleText: LNbits rushes emergency patch after reported Bitcoin wallet thefts The project warned that installations running older versions were vulnerable and urged operators to replace potentially exposed credentials even after upgrading. Bitcoin Lightning wallet platform LNbits has urged users to update immediately to its latest version after reporting a wave of attacks targeting LNbits instances that resulted in stolen funds. The project published version 1.7.0 on Tuesday, describing it as a critical release addressing vulnerabilities and strengthening authentication, extension management and payment handling. LNbits warned that updating alone would not protect installations whose credentials had already been compromised. “It’s been a very challenging few days, working relentlessly to get the v1.7 release out after our users and we suffered losses,” LNbits creator Ben Arc said on X. LNbits provides software for running Bitcoin Lightning wallets and payment applications, including merchant checkouts, tipping services and paywalls. Developer Ben Arc said in May that about 200,000 people run the software themselves. LNbits first warned operators on Sunday to disable its Paywall extension while it investigated a potential vulnerability. Just over an hour later, the project urged users to shut down their LNbits servers immediately, citing a wave of attacks. It also took its own hosted installations offline. The company has not yet detailed the exploit and how many were impacted by it. In an announcement accompanying the emergency patch, LNbits said the vulnerability affects all versions before 1.7.0 and puts funds at risk of theft. Related: BitMart founder says security team ‘severely understaffed’ after new hack It also warned that credentials exposed before upgrading could still give attackers access afterward, urging operators to reset wallet keys, replace funding-source credentials and treat secrets stored in LNbits settings as compromised and recommended moving to a fresh server if a compromise is suspected. Cointelegraph reached out to Ben Arc and LNbits for comment. One user, Kevin Ravensberg, said attackers exploited his LNbits instance, withdrawing about 2.3 million satoshis, or 0.023 Bitcoin, through newly created accounts before he could shut down the server. The company said a separate report detailing the exploit would follow. Magazine: Bitcoin’s ‘best buying opportunity ever’ has arrived: Mark Moss

items.summaryTr: Trump welcomes the outcome, praising Hegseth as a "Great American Patriot", but Democrats can try again next year.
items.articleText: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now - Published An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill. A majority of the House of Representatives agreed to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky - for now. In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage". The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump. Massie was the only Republican to vote against moving the resolution to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee on Tuesday. His effort failed in a 211-204 vote, with more than a dozen members, including 11 Democrats, missing the vote. The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress before Democrats take control in January. President Trump celebrated the vote in a post on Truth Social, saying the effort "has miserably FAILED". "Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," Trump said, referring to Hegseth. Massie had previously acknowledged his impeachment bid may not succeed immediately, but argued it could help push Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process. The Kentucky congressman also said that removing Hegseth now would give the Senate time to approve a replacement while Republicans were still in power. Impeachment resolutions can be carried past the end of a congressional term, meaning Democrats would be able to take it up next year. The Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January following a successful midterm election that allowed them control of both chambers. House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, had predicted earlier in the day that the impeachment bid would fail. In the eight articles of impeachment formally introduced in the House on Monday, Massie said Hegseth was "breaking the law and must be held accountable" for fighting a war in Iran for more than 90 days without lawmakers' approval. The impeachment articles also accused Hegseth of overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the US campaign against boats alleged to be carrying drugs in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea. At a news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth called efforts to impeach him a political stunt by a Trump administration opponent who was "disgruntled and defeated". Hegseth also argued Massie's resolution endangered national security, because it communicated to US adversaries "that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations". "This is not patriotism. This is sabotage," he said. He echoed some statements Trump had made during a surprise appearance at the White House briefing room on Monday, including touting a rise in military recruitment levels. But Hegseth said Massie was motivated by policy differences and "not high crimes, not misdemeanours, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offences the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause". Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year to a Trump-backed opponent, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it began in February. He had already incurred the president's ire for demanding the Trump administration release files on deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. While Hegseth has survived politically for now, many lawmakers - including some Republicans - have questioned how long he can last in the administration. Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a Republican, said on Tuesday he expected Hegseth to resign or be fired by Trump. - Published2 days ago

items.titleTr: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
items.summaryTr: The US Department of Justice says the men were involved in a string of plots, including a major incident near the UK airbase that is used by US armed forces.
items.articleText: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says - Published The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe. The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed. One man, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of doing the same from Iran. Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford incident, which came to light when suspicious vans were reported near the base. Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident. Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said. It accuses the trio of planning attacks in Europe that were carried out under the name of a purportedly new group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand - HAYI). "Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK," the DOJ statement said. It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen". Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year. "This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said. He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention. Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah. A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase. No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized. The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot". On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said. In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged. According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel". The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated. "On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base." The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive. "At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added. It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police. - What we know about RAF Fairford counter-terror probe - Published1 October The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident. Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot. The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason. RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades. In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces". items.titleTr: Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war
items.summaryTr: Double amputee Zaher told the BBC last year about his favourite footballer and a dream of being able to walk again.
items.articleText: Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war - Published In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking. The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher. Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer. We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023. More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher. Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again. More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too. The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs. For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again. When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together. "I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins. Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it." Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together." Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer. "Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed". Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF. Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets. Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck. "I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year. She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer." Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes. Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection. "I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time. There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world. Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care. Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war. After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged. For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive. - 'I can't afford to save both twins': Sudan's war left one mother with an impossible choice - Published16 October 2025 - A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan - Published13 November 2025 Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through. "He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself." His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them. As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him. He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home. For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war. The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted. Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine". "I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries. Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows. Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs. items.titleTr: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting
items.summaryTr: The conflict in the Gulf is an opportunity for the US to test its autonomous mine-hunting systems.
items.articleText: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting - Published Traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most dangerous trips a vessel can take. Despite assistance from the US Navy, ships are still being attacked. "To transit the Strait of Hormuz you need agreement between the captain and the crew to take the risk. You need war risk insurance. And the captain has to make the final decision," says Steve Cameron, a former merchant navy officer and maritime consultant. Missiles and drones are a threat from the air, but under the surface mines may also be lurking. "If you're a captain, you'd like to see evidence mines aren't present," Cameron adds. Modern mines rest on the seabed and detonate when they detect an acoustic or magnetic signal, triggering a pressure wave that will break the keel of a passing vessel. Others can rise through shallow waters or float, or be powered towards a target. The technology itself is not difficult or costly, but the mere threat can stop a tanker fleet from sailing. Ian McFarlane of French defence group Thales is a naval architect who knows mine warfare well. "Mines are a very cheap way of waging a naval war, as the Royal Navy is acutely aware," he says. Finding sea mines has traditionally been the job of specialist mine-hunting vessels, with crews of around 80 sailors. To keep humans out of harm's way, an increasing amount of the work is done by systems that are autonomous and monitored from the shore. They might only need 20 personnel, working in shifts on land. With the recruitment and retention challenges facing Nato navies these highly-portable robot systems are very attractive. Such tech has been under development for 20 years. During the 2003 Iraq war the US Navy poked around the seabed looking for mines with a torpedo-shaped robot called the Remus 100. Pinging around with sonar these little machines operated down to around 100ft depth and spared divers a difficult and dangerous task. The latest conflict in the Gulf is testing much more capable systems. The US military is sparing with details about their mine-hunting craft, but we have seen glimpses of them. Iranian forces hauled an uncrewed US autonomous sub, external out of the waters of the Strait of Hormuz in early September. The Pentagon claimed this robot, an Extra Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) from US autonomous defence tech venture Anduril, was a malfunctioning older device with no classified equipment on-board. Whatever its mission, no sailors were imperilled. That, says William Lupton, a naval analyst with Shephard Group, "was a drop in the ocean compared to having prisoners taken", and part of the point of uncrewed vessels. What if an uncrewed vessel is captured? Nato navies are reluctant to go into details, but computer drives can be wiped or destroyed remotely by various means. This may have taken place inside the humming circuit boards of the XLUUV seized by Iran. Such autonomous tech is being embraced by forces around the world. Cooperation between Thales, the Royal Navy, and France's Marine Nationale has produced a robot motor launch. The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle (USV) is packed with sensors programmed to detect mines via sonar that was developed for the oil and gas industries. It tows a 5m long rectangular box, similar to a large torpedo, that takes a hi-resolution look at the seabed and creates a 3D picture refined by AI. The latest mines are designed to blend into their surroundings and the software spots anything that looks like a mine. Autonomous systems are cheaper than conventional minehunters, plus they can be deployed, along with containerised control centres, by air. Steve Prest, associate fellow at the RUSI defence think tank, introduced uncrewed mine hunting into the Royal Navy and was its first fleet robotics officer, a title he acquired in 2014. "There is a bunch of ways to look for a mine using robot boats or robot subs, and while you can't prove the negative, that no mines are there, you can reduce the risk." He says US robot minehunters can either blow up a mine or just mark the spot as somewhere to avoid. "We'll see more use of autonomy but also the missions and capability will expand. And AI will be analysing data from those vessels on the spot as opposed to data being analysed when a drone returns." The Royal Navy recently announced its concept of a hybrid navy - mixing drones with conventional warships. But Prest thinks for this vision to succeed the fleet must operate as one distributed force, sharing data in what he terms a cognitive architecture. The robot only makes a real difference as part of this scheme and it's a mistake to focus on individual uncrewed assets. "Uncrewed or autonomous vessels are not the operating system. They are applications running on it." While robots are on the rise, people are what really matter in the Strait. Neil Roberts speaks for insurers at Lloyd's of London on marine matters and says the psychological impact of the mine threat is inescapable, as is the uncertainty around just how many mines, if any, are out there. "The US says it has cleared the Omani route and believes the mine threat is being managed, with shipments running at about 75% of pre-conflict levels." Fear of the unknown is the most potent aspect of the sea mine threat and robots are now the weapon of choice to confront that fear. Technology of Business - Published28 October - Published23 October - Published9 October

items.title: Stickers and building sets help drive toy sales ahead of Christmas rush
items.summary: A bumper year so far for toy sales comes as debate intensifies over screen time and tech connectivity.

items.titleTr: Stickers and building sets help drive toy sales ahead of Christmas rush
items.summaryTr: A bumper year so far for toy sales comes as debate intensifies over screen time and tech connectivity.
items.articleText: Stickers and building sets help drive toy sales ahead of Christmas rush - Published Traditional games and stickers are helping to drive a bumper year for toy sales, figures show. The data comes ahead of the crucial Christmas run-in for retailers, which peaks at 23 toys sold every second in the UK. The number of toys sold up to October was 17% higher than the same period last year and growth is at a 10-year high, according to research company Circana. The increase comes despite consumers' cost-of-living pressures, and there are signs that some of the biggest growth in sales is for toys priced between £5 and £10. Despite relatively low sales in recent years, the toy sector has been buoyed by sales to "kidults". The kidult market - which is toys and games for those aged over 12 - has been growing, particularly as adults buy toys for themselves. This growth has continued with a 22% increase in the value of sales in the first half of the year. But Melissa Symonds, UK toys director at Circana, said that toys for children - which still represents the majority of sales - had recorded a good year so far. Growing public debate around children's screen time and the role of technology meant squishy toys, stickers and building sets such as Lego were popular. "Connected toys account for less than 1% of market sales, showing that traditional, hands-on play remains overwhelmingly popular," she said. Concerns have been raised about the suitability of some connected devices. A BBC investigation found an AI teddy marketed as being "perfect" for children as young as three said "I can't help with killing you" after seemingly mishearing a question. Meanwhile, debate has intensified about keeping youngsters free from smartphones during the school day. One in five parents of children aged three to nine say the chance to play together as a family influences what they buy, according to market intelligence company The Insights Family. Paul Reader, who chairs the Dream Toys selection panel of retailers and experts across the sector, said that parents wanted to engage with their children's play. "Nothing beats a board game with that. Nothing beats a bit of interaction," he said. 'Shop around but check safety' The panel he chairs has selected a list of toys that retailers believe will be some of the most popular this year. It includes variations on popular toys of recent years, including slime, a soft tiger that roars and grows, and a shark that breaks out of an egg. Symonds said that, despite rising sales in the year so far, nearly half of toy sales came in the build-up to Christmas, and families were still looking closely at costs. There was significant growth in toys priced between £5 and £10, she said. Reader also urged anyone looking for a bargain to shop around, but to ensure that toys were bought from reputable traders so they were genuine and safe. items.summary: The BBC understands the discount chain, which has been edging towards administration, will be given more time to find a buyer.

items.titleTr: Poundland hopeful for last-minute rescue deal to stave off collapse
items.summaryTr: The BBC understands the discount chain, which has been edging towards administration, will be given more time to find a buyer.
items.articleText: Poundland hopeful for last-minute rescue deal to stave off collapse - Published Poundland and its 11,000 employees are hopeful that the retailer's impending collapse can be delayed to allow time for a last-minute rescue deal. The discount chain has been edging towards administration after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts. A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation have told the BBC that they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release of £10m in funding. A committee of MPs is set to question Gordon Brothers, Poundland's US owners, on Wednesday following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal. Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period. The investment firm has denied the claims. But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham. About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops. However, sources close to the matter told the BBC on Tuesday that a release of £10m by its owners, while "small in the scale of things" could help at least postpone the chain's collapse while a longer term solution was explored. Views on Poundland performance differ The 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires on Thursday, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended. Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners. Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget. He added the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where there were losses of £68m. However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading". There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland stores which could mean continuing employment for workers in the event the chain is broken up and sold off in chunks. The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain.

items.summary: The prediction markets operator says the issue involves procedural errors affecting a handful of contracts, many of which weren’t live, according to Politico.

items.titleTr: CFTC warns Kalshi of imminent charges over notification of contracts: Politico
items.summaryTr: The prediction markets operator says the issue involves procedural errors affecting a handful of contracts, many of which weren’t live, according to Politico.
items.articleText: CFTC warns Kalshi of imminent charges over notification of contracts: Politico The prediction markets operator says the issue involves procedural errors affecting a handful of contracts, many of which weren’t live, according to Politico. Prediction markets operator Kalshi is being warned of imminent charges from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission over whether the operator properly notified the agency about new products, Politico reported Tuesday. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating notifications involving dozens of products, the report said, citing a person with direct knowledge of the probe. The agency’s private notification to Kalshi suggests that charges could follow. The investigation has been underway for months, the person said. Speaking to Politico, Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana described the matter as a procedural error involving submissions for a handful of contracts, many of which never went live. “We are already addressing the issue,” she added. The potential enforcement action comes as the CFTC fights to establish its exclusive authority over prediction markets, including by challenging state efforts to regulate Kalshi. Separately, Kalshi is backing the regulator in a separate legal battle over its authority. On Monday, the company joined Coinbase and four other firms in seeking permission to file a brief supporting the CFTC’s treatment of perpetual futures tied to individual US stocks. Related: Coinbase, Kalshi join lawsuit backing CFTC over US stock perp futures

items.titleTr: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
items.summaryTr: The appointment was made after it emerged Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman believed to be a spy for China.
items.articleText: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair - Published Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy. Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing. Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe. The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday. Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools. It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race. Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia. Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked. Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern. - What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy - Published5 hours ago According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China". US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him. However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing. The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary. When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe. Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce. Joon Kim is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focusing on fraud and other criminal acts. The Nvidia investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with the company. He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity. It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang. A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI. - Published18 hours ago

Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools. It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race. Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia. Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked. Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern. - What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy - Published5 hours ago According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China". US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him. However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing. The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary. When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe. Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce. Joon Kim is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focusing on fraud and other criminal acts. The Nvidia investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with the company. He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity. It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang. A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI. - Published18 hours ago

items.articleText: ABD'de Nvidia krizi siyasete sıçradı! Trump'a 'ulusal güvenliği tehlikeye attı' suçlaması - ABD Senatosu Demokrat Lideri Schumer, Trump'ı Nvidia CEO'su Jensen Huang hakkındaki casusluk iddialarına rağmen harekete geçmemekle suçladı. Kongre'de şirketin Çin'e çip satışları ve ulusal güvenlik bağlantılı faaliyetleri mercek altında. ABD Senatosu Demokrat Azınlık Lideri Chuck Schumer, Başkan Donald Trump'ı Nvidia CEO'su Jensen Huang hakkındaki casusluk bağlantılı iddialara rağmen şirket yöneticisini savunmakla suçladı. Schumer, Trump'ın ulusal güvenlik yerine Huang'ın çıkarlarını koruduğunu öne sürerken, Kongre'de Nvidia hakkında kapsamlı soruşturma çağrıları giderek artıyor. Schumer: Trump, Çinli casus iddialarına rağmen harekete geçmedi CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle New York Times'ın haberlerine göre Trump'a, Nvidia CEO'su Jensen Huang'ın Çin istihbaratıyla bağlantılı olduğu öne sürülen Megaspeed yöneticisi Alice Huang ile ilişkisi hakkında bir yıldan uzun süre önce bilgi verildi. Schumer, Senato kürsüsünde yaptığı konuşmada Trump'ın bu bilgilere rağmen herhangi bir adım atmadığını savundu. Schumer, "Ulusal güvenlik açısından en önemli şirketlerimizden birinin CEO'sunun Çinli bir casusla ilişkisi olabileceği konuşuluyor ve Trump bu konuda hiçbir şey yapmadı" ifadelerini kullandı. Trump ise pazartesi günü yaptığı açıklamada iddiaları kısa süre önce öğrendiğini ima etmiş ve Jensen Huang'ın Alice Huang'ın casus olduğundan haberi bulunmadığı yönündeki açıklamasına inandığını söylemişti. Nvidia'nın Çin politikası da tartışmanın merkezinde Schumer, Trump'ın bu yılın başlarında Huang'ı Pekin'e gerçekleştirdiği devlet ziyaretine davet ettiğini ve Nvidia CEO'sunun tavsiyesini dikkate alarak Çin'in bazı gelişmiş yapay zeka çiplerine erişimine izin verdiğini öne sürdü. Demokrat lider ayrıca Nvidia'nın Trump'ın tartışmalı Beyaz Saray balo salonu projesine 25 milyon dolar bağış yaptığını hatırlattı. Schumer, ABD'nin en gelişmiş yapay zeka çiplerinin potansiyel rakip ülkelerin eline geçmemesi gerektiğini belirterek, ihracat kısıtlamalarının gevşetilmesinde Nvidia'nın etkisinin araştırılmasını istedi. Cumhuriyetçiler de Huang'dan açıklama bekliyor Temsilciler Meclisi Çin Komitesi Başkanı Cumhuriyetçi John Moolenaar da Jensen Huang'ın Alice Huang ile ilişkisine ilişkin kapsamlı bir şirket içi soruşturma yürütülmesi gerektiğini söyledi. Moolenaar, Huang'ın Çinli bir istihbarat görevlisiyle hassas bilgiler paylaşıp paylaşmadığının, Çin'e çip satışlarının engellenmesine karşı lobi faaliyetlerinde etkilenip etkilenmediğinin ve Çinli şirketlere Nvidia'nın sınırlı sayıdaki gelişmiş çiplerinin satın alınmasında öncelik tanınıp tanınmadığının açıklığa kavuşturulmasını istedi. Moolenaar, soruşturmanın yalnızca bir hasar kontrolü çalışmasına dönüşmesi halinde kamuoyunun güveninin sağlanamayacağını ifade etti. Cumhuriyetçi Temsilci Brian Mast da Huang'a yöneltilecek sorular arasında Nvidia çiplerinin hangi şirketlere satıldığı, Megaspeed'in bu çipleri hangi amaçla kullandığı ve Nvidia donanımlarına uzaktan kimlerin eriştiği konularının bulunduğunu belirtti. Kongre'de soruşturma baskısı artıyor Huang'ın Kongre'ye bilgi vermesi talebi, her iki partiden milletvekillerinin desteğini alıyor. Cumhuriyetçi Brian Mast, John Moolenaar ve Rick Crawford, 5 Kasım'da Huang'a ortak bir mektup göndererek Çin Komitesi, Temsilciler Meclisi Dış İlişkiler Komitesi ve İstihbarat Komitesi'ne bilgi vermesini istemişti. Demokratların ocak ayında Temsilciler Meclisi ve Senato'da çoğunluğu devralmasıyla Nvidia ve Huang hakkındaki incelemelerin daha da genişlemesi bekleniyor. Schumer ayrıca Çin'in gelişmiş Amerikan teknolojilerine erişimini sınırlandırmayı amaçlayan AI OVERWATCH Act, MATCH Act ve Chip Security Act adlı yasa tasarılarının geçirilmesi için Cumhuriyetçilere çağrıda bulundu. Nvidia Yönetim Kurulu'nun da Huang hakkındaki iddialar ve şirket sırları ile ulusal güvenliğin tehlikeye girip girmediği konusunda bağımsız soruşturma başlattığı açıklanmıştı.

items.articleText: Here’s what happened in crypto today Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation. Today in crypto, hotter-than-expected US inflation raised concerns about a larger Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December, Coinbase and Kalshi joined four other firms backing the CFTC in a lawsuit over single-stock perpetual futures, and cybersecurity firm CertiK urged crypto exchanges to impose hard dollar limits on hot-wallet holdings. Hot US inflation raises odds of half-point Fed hike in December Crypto industry experts warned on Tuesday that higher-than-expected US inflation could lead to a another Federal Reserve interest rate hike, making borrowing more expensive and potentially discouraging investment in cryptocurrencies. The US Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.4% month over month in October, above economists’ forecast of 0.3%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics - a slower increase than September’s 0.6% rise. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, above the expected 0.2%. Currently, the Federal Reserve holds its benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4.00%, after raising it by a quarter-point in September and leaving it unchanged in October. The report came just a few hours after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said in London that another core inflation reading of 0.3% or higher could prompt the Fed to consider a larger interest rate hike in December. “In that case, I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting,” Waller said. “Hiking only 25-basis-points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.” Coinbase, Kalshi join lawsuit backing CFTC over US stock perp futures Coinbase, Kalshi and four other companies asked a federal court Monday to accept a brief backing the United States Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) in a lawsuit over perpetual futures tied to individual US stocks. According to a proposed amicus brief shared Monday by Coinbase legal representative Molly Abraham, the group also includes Kraken parent Payward, trading companies DRW Holdings and Jump Trading, and crypto investment company Paradigm Operations. The companies argue that stock perpetual futures fall under existing US futures laws. The filing comes days after a federal judge found that the CFTC likely “exceeded its statutory authority” in allowing single-stock perpetuals to trade as security futures. The case could determine whether US exchanges can offer retail traders contracts that track individual stocks without expiring. On Nov. 3, the CFTC announced that single-stock perpetual futures, or stock perps, could begin trading on US-regulated exchanges for the first time. The Capital Markets Alliance Association (CMAA), a newly formed trade and advocacy group representing traditional financial market participants and whose members include Cboe and Citadel Securities, sued the CFTC last week, challenging the CFTC’s authority to allow the contracts to trade. Crypto exchanges need dollar caps on hot wallets, CertiK says Crypto exchanges should impose hard dollar limits on their hot-wallet holdings rather than relying solely on cold-storage ratios to measure security, according to cybersecurity firm CertiK. The recommendation came as several crypto exchanges recently disclosed how much they held in cold wallets, seeking to reassure customers after the record Binance hack that targeted its hot wallets. Crypto exchange Gate reported that 88.26% of its total assets were in cold storage, while Coinbase said it keeps more than 99% of customer assets offline. “Cold storage is a useful measure of online exposure, but it is not a standalone security score,” CertiK’s research team told Cointelegraph. CertiK said crypto exchanges should consider setting hot-wallet caps for each asset and blockchain according to the strictest of three limits: a percentage of customer liabilities, estimated withdrawal needs and an absolute loss ceiling based on the exchange’s financial resources and recovery capabilities. “Flexibility should support operating liquidity, while hard dollar ceilings and circuit breakers limit potential loss,” they said.

items.summary: Crypto custodians are moving into a market handling billions in daily settlements, but regulatory relief and a shift in congressional control leave questions over their long-term role.

items.titleTr: Can crypto trust firms compete with banks in US derivatives settlements?
items.summaryTr: Crypto custodians are moving into a market handling billions in daily settlements, but regulatory relief and a shift in congressional control leave questions over their long-term role.
items.articleText: Can crypto trust firms compete with banks in US derivatives settlements? Crypto custodians are moving into a market handling billions in daily settlements, but regulatory relief and a shift in congressional control leave questions over their long-term role. Crypto companies are moving deeper into financial services traditionally dominated by banks, seeking a role in US derivatives settlements, where billions of dollars change hands daily. The push comes as regulators expand the services trust companies can provide, even as traditional banking groups challenge parts of the regulatory framework governing crypto firms’ expansion into banklike activities. A Nov. 5 decision by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) illustrates the shift, allowing derivatives clearinghouses to use trust companies for daily settlements with clearing members, a function previously restricted to banks under the agency’s regulations. The relief could create new business opportunities for regulated crypto custodians, but its revocable nature and changes in the US political landscape raise questions about the durability of the regulatory opening. Crypto firms eye billions in daily derivatives settlements The scale of the derivatives settlement business offers some perspective on the opportunity. CME Group, one of the world’s largest derivatives market operators, transferred an average of $8.7 billion per business day through its clearing systems during the first half of 2026, up from $6.7 billion a day in 2025, according to regulatory filings. Those figures represent funds transferred between clearing firms to settle gains and losses, rather than fees earned by settlement banks. They nevertheless illustrate the scale of financial flows supported by the infrastructure that trust companies could increasingly help provide. The CFTC’s Division of Clearing and Risk issued no-action relief on Nov. 5 following an Oct. 29 request from derivatives clearinghouse Nodal Clear, allowing clearinghouses to use trust companies for daily settlements if they meet the same evaluation and monitoring requirements applied to traditional settlement banks. The decision addresses an inconsistency between federal commodities law, which permits customer funds to be held at banks or trust companies, and CFTC Regulation 39.14, which defines settlement banks only as banks. Nodal Clear partnered with Coinbase in 2025 to integrate USDC into US futures trading. Coinbase Custody Trust was already expected to provide daily settlement services under the arrangement, Cointelegraph has learned. Related: CFTC expands regulatory relief for passive trading software providers Other crypto firms have also expanded their institutional financial services. On Nov. 4, BitGo launched its Global Markets division, combining derivatives trading, financing, collateral management and settlement capabilities. Coinbase’s national trust bank charter also took effect on Nov. 6, allowing Coinbase National Trust Company, a separate entity from Coinbase Custody Trust, to provide federally supervised digital asset custody services. Several major crypto firms have also secured US national trust bank approvals over the past months, including Circle, Ripple, Crypto.com and Stripe-owned Bridge. The charters, granted by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), reflect the industry’s expansion into federally regulated financial services. Traditional banks contest crypto firms’ expanding role The expansion of specialized trust companies has prompted objections from traditional banking groups. In October, the Independent Community Bankers of America sued the OCC, arguing that its national trust bank charter rules could allow crypto firms to conduct certain banklike activities without meeting all the requirements imposed on conventional banks. The lawsuit reflects a broader disagreement over how specialized financial institutions should be regulated as they expand into services also provided by banks. Cody Carbone, CEO of The Digital Chamber, told Cointelegraph that the CFTC’s relief does not put trust companies in a better or worse position than traditional banks. Trust companies and banks already compete for services permitted under their respective charters, Carbone said, adding that the decision gives clearinghouses more options without preventing banks from retaining their business. “A trust company charter is not a regulatory shortcut,” he said. Revocable relief faces a changing regulatory landscape Despite the potential opportunities, the CFTC’s decision leaves questions about how securely trust companies can establish a long-term role in derivatives settlement. The agency issued a no-action letter rather than formally amending its regulations. The letter states that CFTC staff will not recommend enforcement action against clearinghouses using trust companies for daily settlements if specified conditions are met. Unlike a formal rule amendment, which generally requires a public notice-and-comment process, staff no-action relief does not change the underlying regulation and can be withdrawn. “A change in Commission leadership could withdraw the CFTC Letter. More formal Commission action, such as amending the regulation, would be necessary to avoid this potential risk,” Jordan Yeagley, a shareholder at Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney, told Cointelegraph. The uncertainty comes at a politically significant moment for the agency. CFTC Chair Michael Selig remains the regulator’s sole commissioner, despite a statutory structure providing for five commissioners. Selig has led the agency since December 2025, leaving four seats vacant as the regulator expands its work on digital asset markets. The political environment is also changing following the Nov. 3 US midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. The incoming Congress, which takes office in January, will have greater power to scrutinize the CFTC’s regulatory agenda. The Senate also has a role in confirming nominees to fill the agency’s vacant commissioner seats, while the House and Senate Agriculture Committees oversee the regulator. Sen. Sherrod Brown, who won Ohio’s Senate race on Nov. 3 despite more than $60 million in opposition spending from crypto-backed political action committees, could take on a prominent role on the Senate Agriculture Committee. The push comes as regulators expand the services trust companies can provide, even as traditional banking groups challenge parts of the regulatory framework governing crypto firms’ expansion into banklike activities. A Nov. 5 decision by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) illustrates the shift, allowing derivatives clearinghouses to use trust companies for daily settlements with clearing members, a function previously restricted to banks under the agency’s regulations. The relief could create new business opportunities for regulated crypto custodians, but its revocable nature and changes in the US political landscape raise questions about the durability of the regulatory opening. Crypto firms eye billions in daily derivatives settlements The scale of the derivatives settlement business offers some perspective on the opportunity. CME Group, one of the world’s largest derivatives market operators, transferred an average of $8.7 billion per business day through its clearing systems during the first half of 2026, up from $6.7 billion a day in 2025, according to regulatory filings. Those figures represent funds transferred between clearing firms to settle gains and losses, rather than fees earned by settlement banks. They nevertheless illustrate the scale of financial flows supported by the infrastructure that trust companies could increasingly help provide. The CFTC’s Division of Clearing and Risk issued no-action relief on Nov. 5 following an Oct. 29 request from derivatives clearinghouse Nodal Clear, allowing clearinghouses to use trust companies for daily settlements if they meet the same evaluation and monitoring requirements applied to traditional settlement banks. The decision addresses an inconsistency between federal commodities law, which permits customer funds to be held at banks or trust companies, and CFTC Regulation 39.14, which defines settlement banks only as banks. Nodal Clear partnered with Coinbase in 2025 to integrate USDC into US futures trading. Coinbase Custody Trust was already expected to provide daily settlement services under the arrangement, Cointelegraph has learned. Related: CFTC expands regulatory relief for passive trading software providers Other crypto firms have also expanded their institutional financial services. On Nov. 4, BitGo launched its Global Markets division, combining derivatives trading, financing, collateral management and settlement capabilities. Coinbase’s national trust bank charter also took effect on Nov. 6, allowing Coinbase National Trust Company, a separate entity from Coinbase Custody Trust, to provide federally supervised digital asset custody services. Several major crypto firms have also secured US national trust bank approvals over the past months, including Circle, Ripple, Crypto.com and Stripe-owned Bridge. The charters, granted by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), reflect the industry’s expansion into federally regulated financial services. Traditional banks contest crypto firms’ expanding role The expansion of specialized trust companies has prompted objections from traditional banking groups. In October, the Independent Community Bankers of America sued the OCC, arguing that its national trust bank charter rules could allow crypto firms to conduct certain banklike activities without meeting all the requirements imposed on conventional banks. The lawsuit reflects a broader disagreement over how specialized financial institutions should be regulated as they expand into services also provided by banks. Cody Carbone, CEO of The Digital Chamber, told Cointelegraph that the CFTC’s relief does not put trust companies in a better or worse position than traditional banks. Trust companies and banks already compete for services permitted under their respective charters, Carbone said, adding that the decision gives clearinghouses more options without preventing banks from retaining their business. “A trust company charter is not a regulatory shortcut,” he said. Revocable relief faces a changing regulatory landscape Despite the potential opportunities, the CFTC’s decision leaves questions about how securely trust companies can establish a long-term role in derivatives settlement. The agency issued a no-action letter rather than formally amending its regulations. The letter states that CFTC staff will not recommend enforcement action against clearinghouses using trust companies for daily settlements if specified conditions are met. Unlike a formal rule amendment, which generally requires a public notice-and-comment process, staff no-action relief does not change the underlying regulation and can be withdrawn. “A change in Commission leadership could withdraw the CFTC Letter. More formal Commission action, such as amending the regulation, would be necessary to avoid this potential risk,” Jordan Yeagley, a shareholder at Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney, told Cointelegraph. The uncertainty comes at a politically significant moment for the agency. CFTC Chair Michael Selig remains the regulator’s sole commissioner, despite a statutory structure providing for five commissioners. Selig has led the agency since December 2025, leaving four seats vacant as the regulator expands its work on digital asset markets. The political environment is also changing following the Nov. 3 US midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. The incoming Congress, which takes office in January, will have greater power to scrutinize the CFTC’s regulatory agenda. The Senate also has a role in confirming nominees to fill the agency’s vacant commissioner seats, while the House and Senate Agriculture Committees oversee the regulator. Sen. Sherrod Brown, who won Ohio’s Senate race on Nov. 3 despite more than $60 million in opposition spending from crypto-backed political action committees, could take on a prominent role on the Senate Agriculture Committee. Magazine: What Democrats’ US midterm sweep means for the CLARITY Act

items.titleTr: Across Protocol warns users to avoid app amid reports of drained wallets
items.summaryTr: The protocol is investigating a potential security incident affecting its domain, while several users have reported losing funds after interacting with the platform.
items.articleText: Across Protocol warns users to avoid app amid reports of drained wallets The protocol is investigating a potential security incident affecting its domain, while several users have reported losing funds after interacting with the platform. Crosschain bridging protocol Across, which allows users to transfer digital assets between Ethereum and other blockchain networks, warned users Tuesday not to access its app or connect their wallets while it investigates a potential security incident. In a Tuesday X post, Across advised users against signing transactions or approvals until further notice, without specifying the nature of the incident or whether its website had been compromised. Source: Across Protocol On X, one user claimed to have lost $9,000 in USDC, while another reported losing 7,053 USDT0 across seven transactions on the Plasma blockchain. A third user said their wallet was drained after using the bridge several times, alleging that the website had been compromised. Across asked the users for transaction details to investigate their reports. Cointelegraph has not independently verified the reports. Across Protocol did not immediately respond to Cointelegraph’s request for more details. Across Protocol responds to user reporting $9,000 USDC loss. Source: X user bilm01 NEAR AI discloses separate security breach In a separate security incident, NEAR AI disclosed Monday that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its AI infrastructure, exposing account details belonging to approximately 100 users and data from 18 AI agents. According to a Nov. 9 incident report, attackers exploited a remote code execution vulnerability in SGLang, an open-source AI inference engine, to gain access to an internal server and other infrastructure. The compromised data included user names, email addresses, agent chat histories, settings and logs, while two customers had API keys exposed. NEAR AI said attackers may also have observed requests processed on the compromised server, including those running in confidential mode. The company said it had patched the vulnerability, revoked exposed credentials and restored access to its cloud services. Magazine: Vitalik ‘pivots’ ETH to store of value, crypto suffers after US midterms: Hodler’s Digest
